Near-Gaussian counterexamples to the Ball–Nayar–Tkocz entropy concavity conjecture

Congyi Luo Address: School of Data Science, Fudan University, Shanghai 200433, China Email address: cyluo24@m.fudan.edu.cn
Abstract.

The Ball–Nayar–Tkocz conjecture asserts that, for independent real random variables X,YX,Y with a common log-concave density, the function t↦h⁡(t​X+1−t​Y)t\mapsto h(\sqrt{t}X+\sqrt{1-t}Y) is concave on [0,1][0,1]. Gaussian distributions have this property. We construct strongly log-concave counterexamples arbitrarily close to the Gaussian and study their persistence under Gaussian smoothing. Let XX have mean zero and variance one, let GG be an independent standard Gaussian, and let q∈[0,1]q\in[0,1] denote the signal variance proportion in the smoothed variable q​X+1−q​G\sqrt{q}X+\sqrt{1-q}G. In the asymmetric case, for every fixed 0<q≤10<q\leq 1, there are counterexamples for which the entropy of the weighted sum of two independent copies of the smoothed variable has strictly positive second derivative near the endpoints. In the symmetric case, for every 4/7<q≤14/7<q\leq 1, there are counterexamples for which an unequally weighted sum has strictly greater entropy than the equally weighted sum. Both families have smooth, strictly positive densities and are strongly log-concave before and after smoothing. The density ratios f/φf/\varphi converge uniformly to one, and each derivative of fixed positive order converges uniformly to zero, where φ\varphi is the standard Gaussian density. The symmetric counterexamples can also match any prescribed finite number of Gaussian moments exactly. The asymmetric construction uses an endpoint expansion of entropy, whereas the symmetric construction exploits the different decay rates of high-order Hermite perturbations under different weights. Thus, densities violating concavity approach the Gaussian density in the strong sense described above. The question of uniform concavity in the symmetric class for 0<q≤4/70<q\leq 4/7 remains open.

Key words and phrases: 
Differential entropy, strongly log-concave densities, Gaussian smoothing, Hermite polynomials, interpolation inequalities

1. Introduction and main theorems

Let X,YX,Y be independent real random variables with common density ff, and write

h(X)=−∫ℝflogf,Ff(t)=h(tX+1−tY),0≤t≤1.h(X)=-\int_{\mathbb{R}}f\log f,\qquad F_{f}(t)=h(\sqrt{t}X+\sqrt{1-t}Y),\quad 0\leq t\leq 1.

Throughout, logarithms are natural, and every entropy considered is required to have an absolutely integrable integrand f​log⁡ff\log f. Ball, Nayar, and Tkocz [2, Conjecture 2] ask whether FfF_{f} is concave whenever ff is log-concave. This normalization keeps the variance of the weighted sum fixed. Since Ff​(t)=Ff​(1−t)F_{f}(t)=F_{f}(1-t), concavity necessarily implies

(1.1) Ff​(1/2)≥12​{Ff​(t)+Ff​(1−t)}=Ff​(t).F_{f}(1/2)\geq\tfrac{1}{2}\{F_{f}(t)+F_{f}(1-t)\}=F_{f}(t).

For a Gaussian density ff, the function FfF_{f} is constant. Two questions therefore arise: does concavity hold in some neighborhood of the Gaussian, and does Gaussian smoothing with a fixed proportion suffice to ensure concavity? We give counterexamples to both assertions, distinguishing symmetric and asymmetric inputs.

Write φ(x)=(2π)−1/2e−x2/2\varphi(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^{2}/2}. For a density ff with mean zero and variance one, let

Xq=q​X+1−q​G,0≤q≤1,X_{q}=\sqrt{q}X+\sqrt{1-q}G,\qquad 0\leq q\leq 1,

where X∼fX\sim f and GG is an independent standard Gaussian, and denote the density of XqX_{q} by 𝒮q​f\mathcal{S}_{q}f. The parameter qq is the fraction of the total variance contributed by the signal: q=1q=1 gives the original distribution, whereas q=0q=0 gives the standard Gaussian. We study F𝒮q​fF_{\mathcal{S}_{q}f}, the entropy of the weighted sum of two independent copies of the smoothed input. We prove that asymmetric counterexamples arbitrarily close to the Gaussian exist for every 0<q≤10<q\leq 1, and symmetric ones exist for every 4/7<q≤14/7<q\leq 1. Both families approach the Gaussian uniformly in relative density and in derivatives of every fixed order, and remain strongly log-concave before and after smoothing. The symmetric counterexamples can also match any prescribed finite number of Gaussian moments exactly. The symmetric case 0<q≤4/70<q\leq 4/7 remains unresolved; we do not establish 4/74/7 as a critical value for entropy concavity.

1.1. Main theorems

For a smooth function uu, write

∥u∥Cbm=max0≤j≤msupx∈ℝ|u(j)(x)|,m=0,1,2,….\|u\|_{C_{b}^{m}}=\max_{0\leq j\leq m}\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}}|u^{(j)}(x)|,\qquad m=0,1,2,\ldots.

A strictly positive C2C^{2} density ff is called strongly log-concave if (log⁡f)′′≤−c(\log f)^{\prime\prime}\leq-c for some c>0c>0. All convergence of relative densities below means convergence in CbmC_{b}^{m} for every fixed mm.

Theorem 1.1 (Asymmetric counterexamples: 0<q≤10<q\leq 1).

Fix 0<q≤10<q\leq 1. There exists a sequence (fn)(f_{n}) of strictly positive, smooth, asymmetric probability densities, each with mean zero and variance one, such that:

  1. (i)

    Strict convexity near the endpoint. For every sufficiently large nn, there exists δn∈(0,1/2)\delta_{n}\in(0,1/2) such that

    (1.2) F𝒮q​fn′′​(t)>0,0<t<δn.F_{\mathcal{S}_{q}f_{n}}^{\prime\prime}(t)>0,\qquad 0<t<\delta_{n}.
  2. (ii)

    Strongly log-concave approximation of the Gaussian. Both fnf_{n} and 𝒮q​fn\mathcal{S}_{q}f_{n} are strongly log-concave, and

    ‖fnφ−1‖Cbm⟶0,‖𝒮q​fnφ−1‖Cbm⟶0,m=0,1,2,….\left\|\frac{f_{n}}{\varphi}-1\right\|_{C_{b}^{m}}\longrightarrow 0,\qquad\left\|\frac{\mathcal{S}_{q}f_{n}}{\varphi}-1\right\|_{C_{b}^{m}}\longrightarrow 0,\qquad m=0,1,2,\ldots.

The sequence may depend on the fixed qq. Inequality (1.2) directly contradicts concavity. Thus no fixed positive signal fraction guarantees concavity throughout the general strongly log-concave class. The explicit construction is given in Section 3; the required endpoint expansion is proved in Appendix A.

Theorem 1.2 (Symmetric counterexamples: 4/7<q≤14/7<q\leq 1).

Fix an integer K≥1K\geq 1. There exists a sequence (fn)(f_{n}) of strictly positive, smooth, symmetric probability densities of variance one with the following properties.

  1. (i)

    The equally weighted sum does not maximize entropy. For every 4/7<q≤14/7<q\leq 1, there are tq∈(0,1/2)t_{q}\in(0,1/2), independent of nn, and an integer NqN_{q} such that

    (1.3) F𝒮q​fn​(tq)>F𝒮q​fn​(1/2),n≥Nq.F_{\mathcal{S}_{q}f_{n}}(t_{q})>F_{\mathcal{S}_{q}f_{n}}(1/2),\qquad n\geq N_{q}.
  2. (ii)

    Smooth approximation of every fixed order. For every fixed 4/7<q≤14/7<q\leq 1 and integer m≥0m\geq 0,

    (1.4) ‖fnφ−1‖Cbm\displaystyle\left\|\frac{f_{n}}{\varphi}-1\right\|_{C_{b}^{m}} ⟶0,\displaystyle\longrightarrow 0,
    ‖𝒮q​fnφ−1‖Cbm\displaystyle\left\|\frac{\mathcal{S}_{q}f_{n}}{\varphi}-1\right\|_{C_{b}^{m}} ⟶0.\displaystyle\longrightarrow 0.

    Moreover, for sufficiently large nn, the densities before and after smoothing satisfy

    (log⁡fn)′′<−12,(log⁡𝒮q​fn)′′<−12.(\log f_{n})^{\prime\prime}<-\frac{1}{2},\qquad(\log\mathcal{S}_{q}f_{n})^{\prime\prime}<-\frac{1}{2}.
  3. (iii)

    Exact matching of finitely many Gaussian moments. For every 4/7<q≤14/7<q\leq 1, every nn, and j=0,1,…,2​Kj=0,1,\ldots,2K,

    (1.5) ∫ℝxj​fn​(x)​𝑑x\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}x^{j}f_{n}(x)\,dx =∫ℝxj​φ​(x)​dx,\displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}}x^{j}\varphi(x)\,dx,
    ∫ℝxj​(𝒮q​fn)​(x)​𝑑x\displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}}x^{j}(\mathcal{S}_{q}f_{n})(x)\,dx =∫ℝxj​φ​(x)​dx.\displaystyle=\int_{\mathbb{R}}x^{j}\varphi(x)\,dx.

The same sequence (fn)(f_{n}) works for all these qq; its choice depends only on KK.

Inequality (1.3) reverses the necessary condition (1.1) for concavity. Since F𝒮q​fn​(tq)=F𝒮q​fn​(1−tq)F_{\mathcal{S}_{q}f_{n}}(t_{q})=F_{\mathcal{S}_{q}f_{n}}(1-t_{q}), it gives a strict violation at a pair of weights symmetric about the midpoint. Taking q=1q=1 gives symmetric counterexamples to the Ball–Nayar–Tkocz conjecture while retaining the approximation and moment constraints in (ii) and (iii).

Remark 1.3 (Comparison weights and uniformity in the parameter).

The comparison weights in Theorem 1.2 can be chosen on either side of the midpoint. For every fixed 4/7<q≤14/7<q\leq 1, there exists aq>0a_{q}>0 such that every fixed t∈(0,1)t\in(0,1) satisfying

0<|t−12|<aq0<\left|t-\frac{1}{2}\right|<a_{q}

has F𝒮q​fn​(t)>F𝒮q​fn​(1/2)F_{\mathcal{S}_{q}f_{n}}(t)>F_{\mathcal{S}_{q}f_{n}}(1/2) for all sufficiently large nn. The lower bound on the degree may depend on qq and the chosen tt. Furthermore, for every fixed q0∈(4/7,1]q_{0}\in(4/7,1], a common comparison weight and a common lower bound on the degree can be chosen for q∈[q0,1]q\in[q_{0},1].

Section 8 expresses these approximation properties as boundary statements at the Gaussian density.

1.2. Related results and the proofs

Gaussian scale mixtures provide a class for which the proposed concavity holds. Such variables have the form S​GSG, where S>0S>0 is independent of a standard Gaussian GG. Eskenazis, Nayar, and Tkocz [5, Theorem 8] proved that the equally weighted sum of independent copies of a Gaussian scale mixture maximizes weighted entropy whenever the relevant entropies are finite; Eskenazis and Gavalakis [4, Theorem 1] further proved entropy concavity for weighted sums of two independent Gaussian scale mixtures. Theorem 1.2 shows that the same conclusion fails in the symmetric strongly log-concave class, even arbitrarily close to the Gaussian and under any prescribed finite number of exact Gaussian moment constraints.

The normalization of the weights also affects the direction of entropy comparisons. Yu [12, Theorem 1] proved that, for independent copies of a log-concave variable,

h⁡(λ​X+(1−λ)​Y)≥h⁡((X+Y)/2),0≤λ≤1.h(\lambda X+(1-\lambda)Y)\geq h((X+Y)/2),\qquad 0\leq\lambda\leq 1.

Here the sum of the coefficients is fixed. We instead fix their squared sum, preserving the variance of the weighted sum; the proposed midpoint inequality is (1.1).

Madiman, Nayar, and Tkocz [8, Theorem 1] studied comparisons involving a fixed copy and a normalized sum of several copies; their counterexample is not the two-copy weight comparison in (1.3). Appendix C gives a more elementary construction with a single cosine, showing directly how equal and unequal weights produce different entropies under convolution.

The asymmetric theorem relies on an endpoint expansion. For a density gg with mean zero and variance one whose relative perturbation of the Gaussian is a Schwartz function, let

μ3​(g)=∫x3​g​(x)​𝑑x,J3​(g)=∫g⁡(x)​((log⁡g)′​(x))3​𝑑x.\mu_{3}(g)=\int x^{3}g(x)\,dx,\qquad J_{3}(g)=\int g(x)\bigl((\log g)^{\prime}(x)\bigr)^{3}\,dx.

Under the assumptions of Appendix A, we prove

Fg′′​(t)=−μ3​(g)​J3​(g)16​t+O⁡(1),t↓0.F_{g}^{\prime\prime}(t)=-\frac{\mu_{3}(g)J_{3}(g)}{16\sqrt{t}}+O(1),\qquad t\downarrow 0.

Thus μ3​(g)​J3​(g)<0\mu_{3}(g)J_{3}(g)<0 suffices to give strictly positive curvature near the endpoint. The construction takes the form fε=φ⁡(1+ε​u+ε2​dq​v)f_{\varepsilon}=\varphi(1+\varepsilon u+\varepsilon^{2}d_{q}v): the fourth and fifth Hermite components of uu preserve the first three moments and produce the required contribution to the third moment of the logarithmic derivative; the third-order component of vv adjusts the third central moment. For fixed q>0q>0, we choose dqd_{q} so that the smoothed density satisfies μ3​(g)>0\mu_{3}(g)>0 and J3​(g)<0J_{3}(g)<0, and then choose ε\varepsilon sufficiently small to retain strong log-concavity. Section 3 gives this choice and controls the remainder.

For symmetric densities, μ3​(g)=J3​(g)=0\mu_{3}(g)=J_{3}(g)=0, so this endpoint term vanishes. We instead use Hermite functions of high degree at a fixed spatial scale and cancel finitely many low-order moments. The relative perturbation of the convolution density splits into terms linear and quadratic in the amplitude. Mehler’s formula gives an exact generating function for the linear term; a four-variable Gaussian integral and comparison of positive coefficients give upper and lower bounds for the quadratic term. When q>4/7q>4/7, the quadratic term dominates the linear term at the midpoint, whereas at a fixed nearby nonmidpoint weight it has additional exponential decay. The linear term and the moment correction do not alter this comparison. Converting the norm comparison of relative perturbations into an entropy comparison gives (1.3).

Section 9 summarizes the two families and the boundary properties at the Gaussian; Section 10 asks about uniform concavity, local concavity near the Gaussian, and midpoint curvature. Appendices A–B establish the endpoint expansion and moment estimates used in the asymmetric theorem. Appendices C–D extend the single-cosine example to general periodic waveforms and derive a scaling limit near the midpoint; Appendix E then studies the second derivative at the midpoint directly. The Gaussian interpolation theorem in Appendix F explains the appearance of 4/74/7 in the comparison of linear and quadratic terms; its parameter boundary is not asserted to be a sufficient condition for entropy concavity.

2. Gaussian smoothing and Hermite functions

The proofs of both main theorems reduce the sign of entropy differences or derivatives to explicit perturbation estimates. We establish two-sided quadratic bounds for relative entropy and compute a generating function for Gaussian smoothing of Hermite functions. The former reduces entropy comparisons at equal variance to comparisons of Gaussian L2L^{2} norms; the latter gives an exact expression for these norms as the degree varies. Bounds for Hermite derivatives ensure that the small perturbations below remain positive and strongly log-concave. We first introduce the entropy bounds and smoothing operator common to both constructions, and then the Hermite estimates needed for the symmetric construction. Section 3 uses only the first part and the finite-degree polynomials in the appendices. For convenience, ∥⋅∥2\|\cdot\|_{2} below denotes the norm in L2​(ℝ,φ​(x)​d​x)L^{2}(\mathbb{R},\varphi(x)\,dx), and GG always denotes a standard Gaussian variable. If p=φ⁡(1+r)p=\varphi(1+r) is a probability density with ‖r‖∞≤η<1\|r\|_{\infty}\leq\eta<1, define D(p∥φ)=∫plog(p/φ)D(p\|\varphi)=\int p\log(p/\varphi). For comparisons of relative entropy and quadratic divergence under bounded density ratios, see [11, Section IV]; the constants needed here follow from the integral form of Taylor’s formula below.

Lemma 2.1.

Under the preceding assumptions,

‖r‖L2​(φ​d​x)22​(1+η)≤D(p∥φ)≤‖r‖L2​(φ​d​x)22​(1−η).\frac{\|r\|_{L^{2}(\varphi\,dx)}^{2}}{2(1+\eta)}\leq D(p\|\varphi)\leq\frac{\|r\|_{L^{2}(\varphi\,dx)}^{2}}{2(1-\eta)}.

If pp has mean zero and variance one, then h(p)=12log(2πe)−D(p∥φ)h(p)=\frac{1}{2}\log(2\pi e)-D(p\|\varphi).

Proof.

Since ∫φ​r=0\int\varphi r=0, Taylor’s formula with integral remainder gives

D(p∥φ)=∫φ(x)r(x)2{∫011−s1+s​r​(x)ds}dx.D(p\|\varphi)=\int\varphi(x)r(x)^{2}\left\{\int_{0}^{1}\frac{1-s}{1+sr(x)}\,ds\right\}\,dx.

The inner integral lies between 1/[2​(1+η)]1/[2(1+\eta)] and 1/[2​(1−η)]1/[2(1-\eta)]. The positive upper and lower bounds on p/φp/\varphi also bound p​|log⁡p|p|\log p| by a Gaussian density times a quadratic polynomial, so the entropy is finite. Substituting logφ=−log(2π)/2−x2/2\log\varphi=-\log(2\pi)/2-x^{2}/2 into the definition of relative entropy gives the last identity. ∎

We use the probabilists’ convention for Hermite polynomials:

ex​z−z2/2=∑n=0∞Hn​(x)​znn!.e^{xz-z^{2}/2}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}H_{n}(x)\frac{z^{n}}{n!}.

Let φs\varphi_{s} denote the centered Gaussian density of variance ss. For 0≤ρ≤10\leq\rho\leq 1, define

Tρ​g​(x)=𝔼​g​(ρ​x+1−ρ2​G).T_{\rho}g(x)=\mathbb{E}g(\rho x+\sqrt{1-\rho^{2}}G).

If XX has density φ⁡(1+g)\varphi(1+g), then q​X+1−q​G\sqrt{q}X+\sqrt{1-q}G has density φ⁡(1+Tq​g)\varphi(1+T_{\sqrt{q}}g). Indeed, let U,VU,V be standard Gaussians with correlation ρ\rho. The conditional law U|V=xU\mid V=x is N⁡(ρ​x,1−ρ2)N(\rho x,1-\rho^{2}). Weighting the joint Gaussian density by 1+g⁡(U)1+g(U) gives VV the relative density 1+Tρ​g1+T_{\rho}g. Exchanging U,VU,V also shows that TρT_{\rho} is self-adjoint on L2​(φ)L^{2}(\varphi). Conditional Jensen’s inequality and invariance of the Gaussian marginals give ∫|Tρ​g|2​φ≤∫Tρ​(|g|2)​φ=∫|g|2​φ\int|T_{\rho}g|^{2}\varphi\leq\int T_{\rho}(|g|^{2})\varphi=\int|g|^{2}\varphi. The definition also gives Tρ​Tσ=Tρ​σT_{\rho}T_{\sigma}=T_{\rho\sigma}, because the two independent Gaussian noises combine to have variance 1−ρ2​σ21-\rho^{2}\sigma^{2}. The operator contracts both L2​(φ)L^{2}(\varphi) and L∞L^{\infty} norms, and satisfies ‖(Tρ​g)(m)‖∞≤ρm​‖g(m)‖∞\|(T_{\rho}g)^{(m)}\|_{\infty}\leq\rho^{m}\|g^{(m)}\|_{\infty}. When the corresponding derivative of gg is bounded, dominated convergence justifies differentiation under the expectation. The Hermite generating function further gives Tρ​Hj=ρj​HjT_{\rho}H_{j}=\rho^{j}H_{j}: applying TρT_{\rho} to ez​x−z2/2e^{zx-z^{2}/2} gives eρ​z​x−ρ2​z2/2e^{\rho zx-\rho^{2}z^{2}/2}, and one compares coefficients. This diagonalization of Gaussian convolution also appears in Abbe–Zheng [1].

Lemma 2.2.

Let a>0a>0 and

hn,a(x)=2e−ax2/2Hn​(2​a​x)n!.h_{n,a}(x)=\sqrt{2}e^{-ax^{2}/2}\frac{H_{n}(\sqrt{2a}x)}{\sqrt{n!}}.

Then ‖hn,a‖∞≤Bn:=2​e​(n+1)1/4\|h_{n,a}\|_{\infty}\leq B_{n}:=\sqrt{2e}(n+1)^{1/4}, and the norm of every fixed-order derivative grows at most polynomially in nn. In particular, ‖hn,a′′‖∞≤a⁡(2​n+2)​Bn+2\|h_{n,a}^{\prime\prime}\|_{\infty}\leq a(2n+2)B_{n+2}.

Proof.

Mehler’s identity ([9, Eq. 18.18.28], converted using Hnprob(x)=2−n/2Hnphys(x/2)H_{n}^{\rm prob}(x)=2^{-n/2}H_{n}^{\rm phys}(x/\sqrt{2})) reads

∑j≥0rj​Hj​(x)​Hj​(y)j!=11−r2​exp⁡(2​r​x​y−r2​(x2+y2)2​(1−r2)),|r|<1.\sum_{j\geq 0}\frac{r^{j}H_{j}(x)H_{j}(y)}{j!}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-r^{2}}}\exp\!\left(\frac{2rxy-r^{2}(x^{2}+y^{2})}{2(1-r^{2})}\right),\quad|r|<1.

∑j≥0rj​hj,a​(u)2=21−r2​exp⁡(−a​1−r1+r​u2).\sum_{j\geq 0}r^{j}h_{j,a}(u)^{2}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{1-r^{2}}}\exp\!\left(-a\frac{1-r}{1+r}u^{2}\right).

hn,a′=a/2​(n​hn−1,a−n+1​hn+1,a).h_{n,a}^{\prime}=\sqrt{a/2}\bigl(\sqrt{n}\,h_{n-1,a}-\sqrt{n+1}\,h_{n+1,a}\bigr).

Terms with negative indices are understood to be zero. Iterating mm times gives at most 2m2^{m} terms, each with coefficient at most (a/2)m/2​(n+m)m/2(a/2)^{m/2}(n+m)^{m/2}. Thus, for n+m≥1n+m\geq 1,

‖hn,a(m)‖∞≤(2​a)m/2​(n+m)m/2​Bn+m.\|h_{n,a}^{(m)}\|_{\infty}\leq(2a)^{m/2}(n+m)^{m/2}B_{n+m}.

In particular,

hn,a′′=a2​{n⁡(n−1)​hn−2,a−(2​n+1)​hn,a+(n+1)​(n+2)​hn+2,a}.h_{n,a}^{\prime\prime}=\frac{a}{2}\{\sqrt{n(n-1)}h_{n-2,a}-(2n+1)h_{n,a}+\sqrt{(n+1)(n+2)}h_{n+2,a}\}.

Using n⁡(n−1)≤n\sqrt{n(n-1)}\leq n, (n+1)​(n+2)≤n+2\sqrt{(n+1)(n+2)}\leq n+2, and monotonicity of BjB_{j} gives the stated second-derivative bound. ∎

Lemma 2.3.

For 0≤r≤10\leq r\leq 1, in a neighborhood of z=0z=0,

∑n≥0zn​‖Tr​hn,a‖22=2(1+a)2−a2​r2​1(1−τa​(r)​z)​(1−νa​(r)​z),\sum_{n\geq 0}z^{n}\|T_{\sqrt{r}}h_{n,a}\|_{2}^{2}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{(1+a)^{2}-a^{2}r^{2}}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{(1-\tau_{a}(r)z)(1-\nu_{a}(r)z)}},

where

τa​(r)=1−a+a​r1+a−a​r,νa​(r)=a−1+a​r1+a+a​r.\tau_{a}(r)=\frac{1-a+ar}{1+a-ar},\qquad\nu_{a}(r)=\frac{a-1+ar}{1+a+ar}.
Proof.

Let U,VU,V be standard Gaussians with correlation rr. Then ‖Tr​hn,a‖22=𝔼​hn,a​(U)​hn,a​(V)\|T_{\sqrt{r}}h_{n,a}\|_{2}^{2}=\mathbb{E}h_{n,a}(U)h_{n,a}(V). Integrating Mehler’s formula and using the independent coordinates S=(U+V)/2S=(U+V)/\sqrt{2} and D=(U−V)/2D=(U-V)/\sqrt{2}, of variances 1+r1+r and 1−r1-r, respectively, gives

21−z2​𝔼​exp⁡[−a2​1−z1+z​S2−a2​1+z1−z​D2].\frac{2}{\sqrt{1-z^{2}}}\,\mathbb{E}\exp\!\left[-\frac{a}{2}\frac{1-z}{1+z}S^{2}-\frac{a}{2}\frac{1+z}{1-z}D^{2}\right].

Evaluating the one-dimensional Gaussian integrals, the square of the denominator is

(1+a⁡(1+r)+[1−a⁡(1+r)]​z)​(1+a⁡(1−r)+[a⁡(1−r)−1]​z),\bigl(1+a(1+r)+[1-a(1+r)]z\bigr)\bigl(1+a(1-r)+[a(1-r)-1]z\bigr),

Factoring gives the formula. To justify interchanging summation and integration, take |z|≤z0<1|z|\leq z_{0}<1. The preceding lemma and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality give ∑n≥0|z|n​|hn,a​(U)​hn,a​(V)|≤∑n≥0z0n​Bn2<∞\sum_{n\geq 0}|z|^{n}|h_{n,a}(U)h_{n,a}(V)|\leq\sum_{n\geq 0}z_{0}^{n}B_{n}^{2}<\infty, Thus dominated convergence justifies the interchange. 4. Perturbations preserving finitely many Gaussian moments

For a symmetric density, both the third central moment and the third moment of the logarithmic derivative vanish, so the preceding endpoint criterion no longer gives a counterexample. We now construct symmetric densities whose midpoint entropy is strictly smaller. The first step is to satisfy positivity, strong log-concavity, and finite moment constraints simultaneously: for any fixed KK, a finite-dimensional correction of the following high-degree Hermite perturbations matches the Gaussian moments through order 2​K2K exactly and approaches the Gaussian in every fixed-order relative norm. 5. Weighted convolution and the linear term

Having constructed densities satisfying the moment conditions, we determine how far their weighted convolutions depart from the Gaussian. We decompose the output relative density exactly into terms linear and quadratic in the perturbation amplitude, and prove an exponential upper bound for the norm of the linear term. The bound is given in (5.2); comparison with the midpoint lower bound for the quadratic term in the next section determines when the linear term is negligible. Since the two smoothed copies are independent, their combined Gaussian noise has variance 1−q1-q. The full weighted convolution can therefore be represented by a conditional expectation of three independent standard Gaussians.

6. Positive coefficient comparison for the quadratic term

To produce the required entropy gap, the quadratic term must have different sizes at the midpoint and at the comparison weight. Fix q∈[4/7,1]q\in[4/7,1]. We prove that, for every fixed t≠1/2t\neq 1/2 sufficiently close to the midpoint, the ratio of the quadratic norm to its midpoint value tends to zero. The midpoint lower bound and the nonmidpoint upper bound are given in (6.2) and (6.3), respectively. We express the squared norm as a four-variable Gaussian integral and make a complex change of variables so that the generating function has nonnegative coefficients. At the midpoint we retain one term with equal degree in each variable; away from it we bound the sum of coefficients. This gives different exponential decay rates.

7. A strict entropy gap

The preceding sections estimate the linear and quadratic terms. We must still exclude cancellation and show that moment corrections do not change the sign of the entropy gap. For q>4/7q>4/7, we prove that the entropy at a fixed nonmidpoint weight is strictly greater than at the midpoint, completing Theorem 1.2. The estimates also permit a common comparison weight and degree threshold on any compact parameter interval [q0,1]⊂(4/7,1][q_{0},1]\subset(4/7,1]. 8. Consequences of the main theorems

The weighted-sum entropy of the Gaussian is constant, whereas the counterexamples in Theorem 1.2 approach it in relative norms of every order. To express this boundary property, fix K≥1K\geq 1 and let 𝒜K\mathcal{A}_{K} consist of densities satisfying: ff is strictly positive, even, and smooth, (logf)′′≤−1/2(\log f)^{\prime\prime}\leq-1/2, f/φ−1∈Cb∞f/\varphi-1\in C_{b}^{\infty}, infxf⁡(x)/φ⁡(x)>0\inf_{x}f(x)/\varphi(x)>0, and the moments of ff through order 2​K2K agree with the standard Gaussian moments. Here Cb∞=⋂m≥0CbmC_{b}^{\infty}=\bigcap_{m\geq 0}C_{b}^{m}. Give 𝒜K\mathcal{A}_{K} the relative topology determined by the seminorms ‖f/φ−g/φ‖Cbm\|f/\varphi-g/\varphi\|_{C_{b}^{m}}.

For fixed qq, let

𝒞q,K={f∈𝒜K:F𝒮q​f​ is concave on ​[0,1]},\mathcal{C}_{q,K}=\{f\in\mathcal{A}_{K}:F_{\mathcal{S}_{q}f}\text{ is concave on }[0,1]\},
ℳq,K={f∈𝒜K:F𝒮q​f​(t)≤F𝒮q​f​(1/2)​ for all ​t∈[0,1]}.\mathcal{M}_{q,K}=\{f\in\mathcal{A}_{K}:F_{\mathcal{S}_{q}f}(t)\leq F_{\mathcal{S}_{q}f}(1/2)\text{ for all }t\in[0,1]\}.

All these entropies are finite: positive upper and lower bounds on the relative density are preserved by smoothing and conditional expectation, so Gaussian tails control the entropy integrals.

Corollary 8.1.

For every K≥1K\geq 1 and every 4/7<q≤14/7<q\leq 1, the standard Gaussian density φ\varphi belongs to the relative boundaries of both 𝒞q,K\mathcal{C}_{q,K} and ℳq,K\mathcal{M}_{q,K}.

Proof.

Gaussian smoothing and weighted addition with unit squared sum preserve the standard Gaussian distribution, so F𝒮q​φF_{\mathcal{S}_{q}\varphi} is constant. Thus φ∈𝒞q,K⊂ℳq,K\varphi\in\mathcal{C}_{q,K}\subset\mathcal{M}_{q,K}. The densities supplied by the main theorem eventually belong to 𝒜K∖ℳq,K\mathcal{A}_{K}\setminus\mathcal{M}_{q,K} and converge to φ\varphi in every fixed-order relative norm. Every relative neighborhood of φ\varphi therefore meets the complements of both sets. Since φ\varphi itself belongs to both, it is a boundary point of each. ∎

Thus, in the specified relative topology, the Gaussian density is not an interior point of the set where concavity holds. The limiting Gaussian entropy curve is constant and satisfies the concavity inequality with equality; the strict entropy gaps along the approximating sequence tend to zero with the perturbation amplitude. Indeed, uniform convergence of the relative densities and Lemma 2.1 imply uniform convergence to zero of the relative entropies of the weighted sums, and hence of the counterexample gaps. The matching order 2​K2K is fixed before the construction, and the approximating sequence may depend on KK.

Corollary 8.2.

Suppose a fixed q∈[0,1]q\in[0,1] has the property that, for every symmetric, smooth, strongly log-concave density ff of variance one, F𝒮q​fF_{\mathcal{S}_{q}f} is concave. Then q≤4/7q\leq 4/7. Consequently, if smoothing is written as X+σ​GX+\sigma G, a necessary condition for concavity uniformly over all such signals is σ2≥34​Var⁡(X)\sigma^{2}\geq\frac{3}{4}\operatorname{Var}(X).

Proof.

If q>4/7q>4/7, the main theorem directly supplies a density contradicting the assumption. For a signal of variance v>0v>0, center X+σ​GX+\sigma G and divide by v+σ2\sqrt{v+\sigma^{2}}. The signal variance fraction is then q=v/(v+σ2)q=v/(v+\sigma^{2}). This common scaling adds only a weight-independent constant to the entropy curve and therefore does not affect concavity. Solving v/(v+σ2)≤4/7v/(v+\sigma^{2})\leq 4/7 gives the stated necessary condition. ∎

9. Conclusions

We have studied the Ball–Nayar–Tkocz entropy concavity conjecture: if X,YX,Y are independent real random variables with a common log-concave density, is the function

t⟼h⁡(t​X+1−t​Y)t\longmapsto h\!\left(\sqrt{t}\,X+\sqrt{1-t}\,Y\right)

concave on [0,1][0,1]? The square-root weights keep the variance of the weighted sum fixed. For Gaussian inputs this entropy curve is constant and hence concave. We have further asked whether arbitrary proximity to the Gaussian, or Gaussian smoothing with a fixed proportion, suffices to guarantee the same property.

For an input of mean zero and variance one, let qq be the signal variance fraction in q​X+1−q​G\sqrt{q}\,X+\sqrt{1-q}\,G, where GG is an independent standard Gaussian. We proved:

  • •

    Asymmetric inputs: for every 0<q≤10<q\leq 1 there are counterexamples arbitrarily close to the Gaussian, with strictly convex entropy curves near the endpoint.

  • •

    Symmetric inputs: for every 4/7<q≤14/7<q\leq 1 there are counterexamples arbitrarily close to the Gaussian for which an unequally weighted sum has strictly greater entropy than the equally weighted sum.

Both families remain strongly log-concave before and after smoothing, with uniform convergence of relative densities and their derivatives of each fixed order. The symmetric family can also match any prescribed finite number of Gaussian moments exactly. Thus, in these parameter ranges, every relative neighborhood of the Gaussian contains densities violating concavity, even under strong log-concavity and arbitrarily accurate uniform approximation of relative densities and all their fixed-order derivatives.

The Gaussian is consequently not an interior point of the corresponding concavity set; Section 8 establishes this boundary property and the necessary noise lower bound in the symmetric class. Equality at the Gaussian limit is consistent with strict violations along the sequence, since the strict entropy gaps also tend to zero. For symmetric inputs, the range 0<q≤4/70<q\leq 4/7 remains unresolved: 4/74/7 is the boundary of the auxiliary interpolation estimate, not an established critical value for entropy concavity. The remaining question is whether symmetry allows some positive signal fraction to restore concavity, and whether such restoration is possible at least near the Gaussian.

10. Further questions

The main theorems leave a central question: can symmetry allow Gaussian smoothing with a positive signal fraction to restore concavity? We have given asymmetric counterexamples for every positive signal fraction, while the symmetric range 0<q≤4/70<q\leq 4/7 remains unresolved. We distinguish uniform concavity, local properties near the Gaussian, and midpoint curvature.

10.1. Is there a positive range of uniform concavity for symmetric inputs?

Problem 10.1.

Determine all q∈(0,4/7]q\in(0,4/7] for which F𝒮q​fF_{\mathcal{S}_{q}f} is concave for every symmetric log-concave density ff of variance one. In particular, does any q>0q>0 have this property?

If such a positive signal fraction exists, symmetry provides a uniform concavity guarantee unavailable in the general log-concave class. If none exists, symmetric counterexamples persist regardless of the amount of Gaussian noise, provided a positive signal fraction remains. At q=0q=0 the output is always Gaussian, so the question is whether this purely Gaussian case extends to any positive signal fraction.

The value 4/74/7 arises here from the exact parameter boundary of an auxiliary interpolation inequality. For 0<q≤4/70<q\leq 4/7, this inequality prevents the midpoint quadratic term from dominating the linear term for perturbations satisfying the corresponding small-norm condition. It neither determines the sign of the second entropy derivative nor excludes other constructions. Turning this limitation of the method into a concavity theorem, or constructing counterexamples beyond it, are therefore two distinct approaches to the question.

10.2. Can counterexamples still be arbitrarily close to the Gaussian?

Failure of uniform concavity does not imply that counterexamples occur near the Gaussian. Our symmetric counterexamples admit relative approximation of every order and arbitrary finite moment matching. Whether these properties can be retained simultaneously in the remaining parameter range is a stronger question.

Problem 10.2.

Fix q∈(0,4/7]q\in(0,4/7] and an integer K≥1K\geq 1. Do there exist fn∈𝒜Kf_{n}\in\mathcal{A}_{K} such that

‖fn/φ−1‖Cbm⟶0for every fixed ​m≥0,\|f_{n}/\varphi-1\|_{C_{b}^{m}}\longrightarrow 0\qquad\text{for every fixed }m\geq 0,

and F𝒮q​fnF_{\mathcal{S}_{q}f_{n}} fails to be concave for every nn?

Here 𝒜K\mathcal{A}_{K} is the symmetric strongly log-concave class defined in Section 8, whose members match the Gaussian moments through order 2​K2K exactly. The question asks whether the Gaussian can still be approximated by counterexamples under these constraints, or whether some positive signal fractions guarantee concavity in a relative neighborhood of the Gaussian. Such local concavity could hold even if the answer to Problem 10.1 is negative. Distinguishing counterexamples in the entire class from counterexamples near the Gaussian would therefore clarify which properties Gaussian smoothing can restore.

10.3. Can the midpoint entropy comparison be strengthened to strictly positive curvature?

For every q>4/7q>4/7, the main argument makes the midpoint entropy smaller than the entropy of some unequally weighted sum. Appendix E proves the stronger statement F′′​(1/2)>0F^{\prime\prime}(1/2)>0 only for q>2−2q>2-\sqrt{2}. An interval between these parameter ranges is still uncovered.

Problem 10.3.

For every q∈(4/7,2−2]q\in(4/7,2-\sqrt{2}], does there exist a sequence of strictly positive, smooth, symmetric, strongly log-concave densities fnf_{n} with mean zero and variance one, converging to the standard Gaussian in each fixed-order relative CbmC_{b}^{m} norm, such that, for all sufficiently large nn,

F𝒮q​fn′′​(1/2)>0​?F_{\mathcal{S}_{q}f_{n}}^{\prime\prime}(1/2)>0\,?

Since the weighted-sum entropy is symmetric about t=1/2t=1/2, strictly positive curvature would make equal weighting a strict local minimum. This is finer than a two-point entropy comparison and does not follow directly from asymptotic entropy gaps at fixed weights. It requires control of the differentiated error or a new construction allowing exact evaluation of midpoint curvature.

These questions ask, respectively, whether Gaussian smoothing restores concavity throughout the symmetric class, whether it restores concavity only near the Gaussian, and what local shape counterexamples have near equal weighting. An answer to any of them would clarify the roles of symmetry and Gaussian smoothing in entropy concavity.

Appendices

The appendices address concrete questions arising from the two main theorems. Appendices A–B first explain why asymmetric counterexamples can be detected by the opposite signs of two moments, and supply the expansions and estimates used in the main text. We then turn to symmetric constructions: Appendix C gives explicit counterexamples based on a single cosine, while Appendix D extends this phenomenon to general smooth even periodic profiles and computes a scaling limit near the midpoint. This raises two further questions: is the midpoint a strict local minimum, and why does the method of the main text encounter the bound 4/74/7? Appendices E and F answer these questions through curvature calculations and sharp interpolation estimates, respectively. Finally, Appendix G specifies finite parameter values and a strictly positive lower bound for the entropy gap, turning asymptotic existence into an explicit example.

Appendix A Endpoint expansions for asymmetric densities

The asymmetric construction requires a local criterion: which densities make the entropy of the weighted sum strictly convex near the endpoint? We prove that the leading term of the endpoint curvature is determined by the product of the third central moment and the third moment of the logarithmic derivative, namely F′′(t)=−μ3(f)J3(f)/(16t)+O(1)F^{\prime\prime}(t)=-\mu_{3}(f)J_{3}(f)/(16\sqrt{t})+O(1). Thus μ3​(f)​J3​(f)<0\mu_{3}(f)J_{3}(f)<0 suffices to contradict concavity, reducing the construction to adjusting the signs of two integrals. The proof establishes four continuous derivatives of the entropy in the parameter s=ts=\sqrt{t} and then controls the remainder after the change of variables.

Appendix B Moment estimates for asymmetric perturbations

Appendix A reduces the construction to μ3​(f)​J3​(f)<0\mu_{3}(f)J_{3}(f)<0. We explain how to control these factors independently. The fourth and fifth Hermite components preserve the first three moments, while their even–odd cross term changes the third moment of the logarithmic derivative. Adding a third-order component of smaller amplitude then adjusts the third central moment. We give the required vanishing-moment identities, the exact cross integral, and a general cubic remainder bound. These estimates make the sign choices in the main argument strict for every fixed q>0q>0. We use the following three probabilists’ Hermite polynomials:

H3​(y)=y3−3​y,H4​(y)=y4−6​y2+3,H5​(y)=y5−10​y3+15​y.H_{3}(y)=y^{3}-3y,\quad H_{4}(y)=y^{4}-6y^{2}+3,\quad H_{5}(y)=y^{5}-10y^{3}+15y.

Throughout this appendix, u,vu,v are defined by (3.1)–(3.2).

B.1. Moment conditions and the third moment of the logarithmic derivative

The endpoint formula expresses the required sign condition as μ3​(f)​J3​(f)<0\mu_{3}(f)J_{3}(f)<0. To control the factors separately, consider r=ε​u+ε2​vr=\varepsilon u+\varepsilon^{2}v and fε=φ⁡(1+r)f_{\varepsilon}=\varphi(1+r). After the substitution y=2​xy=\sqrt{2}x, the fourth and fifth Hermite polynomials in uu are orthogonal to every polynomial of degree at most three. Thus uu preserves normalization and the first three moments. The third Hermite polynomial in vv preserves normalization, mean, and variance, while increasing the third central moment by 3​ε2/23\varepsilon^{2}/2.

The cross term between the fourth and fifth components determines the quadratic coefficient of the third logarithmic-derivative moment. Identity (B.2) below shows that this coefficient in J3​(fε)J_{3}(f_{\varepsilon}) depends on K=∫x​(u′)2​φK=\int x(u^{\prime})^{2}\varphi. If uu has a single parity, (u′)2(u^{\prime})^{2} is even and the integral vanishes. For our combination the cross term gives K=560​6/27>1K=560\sqrt{6}/27>1, making the coefficient 3​(1−K)3(1-K) negative. The following lemmas derive these moments and identities, before controlling the higher-order remainder.

For the functions in (3.1) and (3.2),

∫xj​u​φ=0(0≤j≤3),∫xj​v​φ=0(0≤j≤2),∫x3​v​φ=3/2.\int x^{j}u\varphi=0\quad(0\leq j\leq 3),\qquad\int x^{j}v\varphi=0\quad(0\leq j\leq 2),\qquad\int x^{3}v\varphi=3/2.

Appendix C An explicit family of cosine counterexamples

The Hermite construction accommodates both noise and moment constraints, but without added noise a simpler counterexample is available. Adding a single cosine mode to the Gaussian density, we prove that for every k≥14k\geq 14 the entropy gap between weights 1/51/5 and 1/21/2 is strictly greater than e−4​k/256e^{-4k}/256. Equal weighting retains a quadratic oscillatory term, whereas the chosen unequal weights exponentially damp all oscillatory terms. This explicit example also motivates the next appendix: does the phenomenon depend on the particular choice of a cosine waveform? We do not normalize the variance here, since common scaling does not affect concavity.

For every real k≥14k\geq 14, let

(C.1) fk​(x)=φ⁡(x)​(1+e−k​cos⁡(k​x))1+e−k−k2/2.f_{k}(x)=\frac{\varphi(x)(1+e^{-k}\cos(kx))}{1+e^{-k-k^{2}/2}}.

Then fkf_{k} is a strictly positive, even, C∞C^{\infty} probability density satisfying (logfk)′′<−1/2(\log f_{k})^{\prime\prime}<-1/2, and

(C.2) Ffk​(1/5)−Ffk​(1/2)>e−4​k256.F_{f_{k}}(1/5)-F_{f_{k}}(1/2)>\frac{e^{-4k}}{256}.

In particular, the midpoint is not a global maximizer of FfkF_{f_{k}}, and FfkF_{f_{k}} is not concave. Moreover, for every fixed nonnegative integer jj,

(C.3) ‖djd​xj(fkφ−1)‖∞⟶0,∥(logfk)′′+1∥∞⟶0(k⟶∞).\left\|\frac{d^{j}}{dx^{j}}\left(\frac{f_{k}}{\varphi}-1\right)\right\|_{\infty}\longrightarrow 0,\qquad\|(\log f_{k})^{\prime\prime}+1\|_{\infty}\longrightarrow 0\quad(k\longrightarrow\infty).

The proof distinguishes the cross terms under equal and unequal weighting. With equal weights, multiplying two cosine factors produces a frequency that is not damped by Gaussian integration. At t=1/5t=1/5, every oscillatory term is exponentially damped. Since the two weighted sums have equal variance, comparing their entropies is equivalent to reversing the comparison of their relative entropies with respect to the standard Gaussian. We first treat amplitude and frequency as independent parameters and then set the amplitude to e−ke^{-k}.

Appendix D Periodic perturbations and a scaling limit near the midpoint

The single-cosine example is not isolated among waveforms. We prove that every nonconstant smooth even periodic waveform, with a suitable small amplitude and high frequency, eventually gives entropy greater than the midpoint entropy at every fixed interior nonmidpoint weight. At fixed weights the entropy deficit is determined by matching integer frequencies, whereas the scale t=1/2+s/kt=1/2+s/k yields a continuous limiting profile. This extension describes both the mechanism of the counterexamples and the scale on which the entropy gap concentrates near the midpoint. We first give explicit bounds for an exponential cosine potential, then treat general waveforms and the scaling limit.

D.1. An exponential cosine potential

The exponential form ensures positivity automatically and reduces log-concavity to an estimate of the second derivative of the potential. With amplitude k−3k^{-3}, it gives an entropy gap greater than 1/(25​k12)1/(25k^{12}) for every k≥10k\geq 10.

Equal weighting retains perturbations of the same frequency in the two inputs, whereas unequal weighting requires matching integer frequency ratios. For instance, when u=cosu=\cos, the normalized midpoint entropy deficit tends to 1/161/16, while the limit at every fixed interior nonmidpoint weight is zero. The threshold for these convergences depends on the weight, and convergence is not uniform near the endpoints; the entropy deficit of the input density at an endpoint is typically of order ϵk2\epsilon_{k}^{2}.

Appendix E Strictly positive midpoint curvature

An entropy value at the midpoint below a nonmidpoint value does not by itself make the midpoint a local minimum; nor does the preceding scaling limit justify interchanging second derivatives. We compute midpoint curvature directly and prove that, for every q>2−2q>2-\sqrt{2}, a Hermite family requiring no moment correction satisfies F′′​(1/2)>0F^{\prime\prime}(1/2)>0. Thus, in this smaller noise range, equal weighting is indeed a strict local minimum. The key is to estimate both the output perturbation and its second derivative with respect to the weight. This construction also matches more Gaussian moments as the degree increases. Let φs\varphi_{s} be the centered Gaussian density of variance ss, let φ=φ1\varphi=\varphi_{1}, and use probabilists’ Hermite polynomials HnH_{n}. Throughout, nn tends to infinity through even integers at least 44.

Appendix F An interpolation inequality for Gaussian smoothing

The symmetric proof requires the midpoint quadratic term to dominate the linear term, producing the restriction 4/74/7. Is this restriction specific to the chosen Hermite sequence, or does it reflect a more general estimate? We prove a Gaussian interpolation inequality for all perturbations in L2​(d​x)L^{2}(dx) and determine its exact parameter range, including the endpoint. At the parameters of the main proof, the inequality shows that for 0<q≤4/70<q\leq 4/7, if the amplitude times the Lebesgue L2L^{2} norm of the perturbation tends to zero, then the midpoint quadratic term is negligible relative to the linear term. This identifies the range of this dominance argument; it does not itself give sufficient conditions for entropy concavity. Two integration measures occur here. We distinguish the Lebesgue norm ∥⋅∥L2​(d​x)\|\cdot\|_{L^{2}(dx)} from the Gaussian norm ∥⋅∥L2​(φ​d​x)\|\cdot\|_{L^{2}(\varphi\,dx)}.

Let 0<r<10<r<1 and 0<s≤10<s\leq 1. There is a finite constant Cr,sC_{r,s} such that every g∈L2​(ℝ,d​x)g\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R},dx) satisfies

(F.1) ‖Ts​g‖L2​(φ​d​x)2≤Cr,s​‖g‖L2​(d​x)​‖Tr​g‖L2​(φ​d​x),\|T_{\sqrt{s}}g\|_{L^{2}(\varphi\,dx)}^{2}\leq C_{r,s}\|g\|_{L^{2}(dx)}\|T_{\sqrt{r}}g\|_{L^{2}(\varphi\,dx)},

if and only if

(F.2) s≤2​r​(1+r)−r.s\leq\sqrt{2r(1+r)}-r.

The range includes equality at the endpoint. The proof is given at the end of this appendix. Taking r=q/2r=q/2 and s=qs=q, condition (F.2) is equivalent to 3​q/2≤q⁡(1+q/2)3q/2\leq\sqrt{q(1+q/2)}, or 0<q≤4/70<q\leq 4/7.

For g∈L2​(d​x)g\in L^{2}(dx), denote the midpoint linear and quadratic conditional expectations by

L⁡(g)=2​Tq/2​g,M⁡(g,g)​(x)=𝔼⁡[g⁡(G1)​g​(G2)∣q/2​(G1+G2)+1−q​G3=x].L(g)=2T_{\sqrt{q/2}}g,\qquad M(g,g)(x)=\mathbb{E}[g(G_{1})g(G_{2})\mid\sqrt{q/2}(G_{1}+G_{2})+\sqrt{1-q}G_{3}=x].

Contraction of conditional expectation gives ‖M⁡(g,g)‖L2​(φ​d​x)≤‖Tq​g‖L2​(φ​d​x)2\|M(g,g)\|_{L^{2}(\varphi\,dx)}\leq\|T_{\sqrt{q}}g\|_{L^{2}(\varphi\,dx)}^{2}: smooth the two independent copies separately and then condition on their equally weighted sum. We obtain the following corollary.

Corollary F.2.

For 0<q≤4/70<q\leq 4/7,

‖M⁡(g,g)‖L2​(φ​d​x)≤12​Cq/2,q​‖g‖L2​(d​x)​‖L⁡(g)‖L2​(φ​d​x).\|M(g,g)\|_{L^{2}(\varphi\,dx)}\leq\tfrac{1}{2}C_{q/2,q}\|g\|_{L^{2}(dx)}\|L(g)\|_{L^{2}(\varphi\,dx)}.

If gn≠0g_{n}\neq 0, ϵn>0\epsilon_{n}>0, and ϵn​‖gn‖L2​(d​x)→0\epsilon_{n}\|g_{n}\|_{L^{2}(dx)}\to 0, then ϵn2​‖M⁡(gn,gn)‖L2​(φ​d​x)/(ϵn​‖L⁡(gn)‖L2​(φ​d​x))→0\epsilon_{n}^{2}\|M(g_{n},g_{n})\|_{L^{2}(\varphi\,dx)}/(\epsilon_{n}\|L(g_{n})\|_{L^{2}(\varphi\,dx)})\to 0.

Proof.

Apply the theorem to the preceding contraction bound. Since φ≤(2π)−1/2\varphi\leq(2\pi)^{-1/2}, we have L2​(d​x)⊂L2​(φ​d​x)L^{2}(dx)\subset L^{2}(\varphi\,dx). In the complete orthonormal basis Hj/j!H_{j}/\sqrt{j!} of L2​(φ​d​x)L^{2}(\varphi\,dx), TρT_{\rho} multiplies the jjth coefficient by ρj\rho^{j}. For ρ=q/2>0\rho=\sqrt{q/2}>0, the equality Tρ​g=0T_{\rho}g=0 forces every coefficient to vanish, hence g=0g=0. The denominator is therefore nonzero for nonzero gng_{n}. Completeness can also be obtained from uniqueness of the Gaussian-weighted Fourier transform: if gg is orthogonal to all polynomials, the entire function z↦∫g⁡(x)​φ​(x)​ez​x​𝑑xz\mapsto\int g(x)\varphi(x)e^{zx}\,dx has all Taylor coefficients zero and is identically zero. Taking purely imaginary zz gives g​φ=0g\varphi=0. Entire analyticity and differentiation under the integral follow from Cauchy–Schwarz and uniform bounds on Gaussian exponential moments over compact sets. ∎

Our moment-corrected Hermite sequence meets this small-norm condition: the original Hermite functions have degree-independent Lebesgue norms, and the fixed-order correction tends to zero exponentially. Thus, for 0<q≤4/70<q\leq 4/7, the midpoint quadratic term is negligible relative to the linear term for sequences satisfying this small-norm condition. This compares only the sizes of the terms; it does not determine the curvature of entropy as a function of the weight. Concavity for symmetric inputs at q≤4/7q\leq 4/7 remains open.

The Gaussian smoothing norm corresponds to a positive integral operator on L2​(d​x)L^{2}(dx). Sufficiency in Theorem F.1 follows from an operator-order comparison of Gaussian kernels; necessity is tested on high-degree Hermite eigenfunctions.
